study.title: 3 John 1 Truth, hospitality and discernment in Christian Communion
study.overview: 3 John is a personal letter and soon in which the author rejoices in Gaius' faithfulness, praises his hospitality to the brothers and those who served the cause of the gospel, warns against the authoritarian posture of Diotrephes and recommends Demetrius as one of good witness. The chapter shows that Christian truth is not only confessed, but lived in love, support for the servants of Christ and rejection of attitudes that divide the church. The letter ends with the expectation of a face-to-face meeting and with affectionate greetings.

outline.title: Greeting and desire for integral prosperity
outline.explanation: The author presents himself as "the elder" and directs an affectionate greeting to Gaius. The desire for material health and well-being accompanies prayer for the prosperity of the soul, showing that the Christian life includes spiritual care and also attention to the person's concrete condition.

outline.title: Joy for Gaio's Loyalty
outline.explanation: The author received a good testimony about Gaius: he walks in the truth. The greatest joy of the leader is to see his spiritual children persevering in the truth of the gospel, which relates Christian maturity to life coherence.

outline.title: Hospitality to the brothers and co-workers of truth
outline.explanation: Gaius is praised for acting faithfully in helping brothers and visitors. These servants went out because of the Name of Christ without relying on the Gentiles, and the church is called to welcome them to share in the work of truth with them.

outline.title: The Contrast between Diotrephes and Demetrius
outline.explanation: Diotrephes is exposed as a domineering, defaming and hostile to the brothers, while Demetrius receives a good general and apostolic testimony. The chapter ends with the exhortation not to imitate evil, but good, and with the hope of a brief meeting in peace.

study.context: The letter presupposes a network of churches and traveling brothers who served in the proclamation of the gospel and received support from believers. The notes indicate that the mentioned church was probably in Ephesus, where the author possibly remained. They also suggest that Demetrius may have been the holder of the letter. These elements help to understand why hospitality, financial support and public testimony are central issues here.
study.theology: The chapter highlights three main theological themes. First, Christian truth is received as apostolic doctrine and also as a way of life; walking in the truth means to remain faithful to the gospel of Jesus Christ. Second, hospitality is a concrete way of participating in the work of God, for those who support the servants of the gospel become a co-worker of truth. Third, leadership in the church should reflect humility and service, not a desire for preeminence; therefore Diotrephes appears as a negative example of selfish power, while Demetrius is presented as one whose life confirms the truth. The letter also shows that peace and fraternal communion belong to the Christian way of life.

scholarViews.insight: The traveling brethren were probably sent from John from church to church, teaching the gospel and encouraging Christians; thus walking in the truth in 3:3 is not simply sincerity, but fidelity to the apostolic gospel.
John's joy in 3:4 shows the pastoral contentment in seeing his spiritual children living in a way consistent with the truth, and this includes practical love and hospitality.

In 3:10, Diotrephes is described as someone who does not receive the brethren, forbids others from welcoming them and even expelling from the church those who wish to do so, which Clarke understands as abuse of authority and opposition to apostolic reception.

questions: What concrete signs show that a person is actually walking in the truth and not just talking about it?
How can my house, my resources and my time serve the brethren and the work of the gospel better?
Is there in me any attitude similar to that of Diotrephes, seeking control, prestige or resistance to correction?
study.practice: This letter calls the Christian to unite truth, love and practical support. A concrete application is to identify a servant of the gospel, missionary, worker or brother in need and offer specific, dignified and responsible help. Another application is to examine one's heart to reject ambition, destructive criticism and closure to the brothers. It is also worth cultivating a whole witness: that our faith can be confirmed not only by words but by a life of obedience, generosity and peace.
study.uncertainty: The given text does not allow to determine with absolute certainty the historical identity of Gaius, Demetrius or Diotrephes, nor does it fix the date of the letter; the reference to Ephesus is an inference of the notes, not an explicit statement of the verse. It is also not possible to conclude, only with these data, additional details about the local situation of the church beyond what the notes indicate.
